coach_says: Before pushing a pawn, look for free material: your bishop on e6 attacks c4, and nothing defends it, so Bxc4 just wins a pawn. Instead d5 opens the centre while your king is still on e8, and after exd5 cxd5 d4 your d5 and e5 pawns are both under fire and start to fall apart. Take what is offered first, and only open the centre once your king is safe.
concept: missed the free pawn on c4
also: opening the centre with king uncastled

coach_says: Your pawn on e5 was a wall on the diagonal from c7 to h2. Pushing it to e6 knocks the wall down: Qc7 now attacks your undefended rook on f4, and the rook can't step away because Qxh2+ comes with the knight on g4. You end up giving the exchange. Before pushing a pawn, ask which lines it was blocking; here d3, developing the c1 bishop and covering the centre, was steady.
concept: pawn push opened a diagonal to h2

coach_says: Your knight on e7 was attacked by the rook on e1 and its only defender was your king. Castling queenside took the king away, so Rxe7 simply wins a knight. Before you move a piece, check what it was protecting. Kd8 or Bb7 kept everything defended.
concept: removed the only defender of e7
also: loose piece on an open file

coach_says: Nc6 puts the knight right in front of White's d-pawn, so d5 hits it and the pawn keeps rolling with tempo: d6, d7, and your pieces are too far away to stop it. In endgames a passed pawn supported by a rook and bishop is very dangerous, and you want your king near it. Kf8 and Ke8 brings the king toward d8 to blockade instead.
concept: knight kicked, passed pawn runs

coach_says: On b4 your knight is attacked by the queen on d2 and defended only by the bishop on c5. White can hit that bishop: Bxe7 Qxe7 d4, and now the bishop is attacked while still having to guard b4, so you lose a piece. When a piece has only one defender, ask whether that defender can be chased away. The knight was attacked by d5xc6, and Nd4 put it on a central square guarded by the e5 pawn.
concept: knight relying on one attackable defender

coach_says: You are a pawn up, but your rook on c8 is stuck guarding c7 while White's rook on c6 eats your pawns (a6 is already loose). Re8 turns things around by attacking the undefended pawn on e4: if Rxc7 then Rxe4 and your rook gets busy too. In rook endgames, an active rook that attacks pawns is usually worth more than a passive one that defends. Kf6 is natural but slower.
concept: activate the rook in rook endgames

coach_says: The knight on c7 forks your king and rook, but you get to choose where the king goes. Kd7 attacks the knight: if Nxa8 then Bxa1 and the knight on a8 is trapped in the corner, and if Rab1 then Kxc7 wins it. Ke7 leaves the knight alone, so White plays Rab1 with tempo on your bishop and then takes on a8 and b7, with check on the seventh rank. When you're forked, look for a king move that attacks the forking piece.
concept: king should attack the forking knight

coach_says: Your king on f2 sits on the diagonal from b6 to g1, and Black is already threatening Qb6+. f4 was the way to meet it: after Qb6+ d4 your knight on e2 still guards d4 and blocks the e-file. Nf4 takes the knight off e2, so after Qb6+ d4 Black swaps on e1, takes the knight with the h6 bishop and the queen gets into b2. When your king is exposed, check the opponent's checks before moving a defender.
concept: ignored the threat Qb6+ on the king
also: moved a key defender off e2

coach_says: e5 puts a pawn on a square your opponent's knight on f3 attacks, and nothing of yours defends it, so Nxe5 wins a pawn and also hits your bishop on g4. Your d4 pawn was the thing under attack; the clean answer was Bxf3, removing the knight that was attacking it. Before pushing a pawn, count who attacks and defends the square it lands on.
concept: pushed a pawn to an undefended square

coach_says: Black's pawn on h2 and queen on h3 have your king boxed in, and the knight on d4 wants to go to f3, where it covers g1; then Qg4 and Qg1+ Rxg1 hxg1=Q is mate. f5 does nothing about that. f3 takes the f3 square away from the knight and frees f2 for your rook. When your king is boxed in, ask which square the enemy pieces need and take it away first.
concept: missed the mating threat Nf3
also: king boxed in by the h2 pawn

coach_says: Your king on g8 sits on an open g-file, and the bishop on h6 controls g7 and f8. White threatens Rg1+ Kh8 Bg7+ Kg8 Bxf6+ and mate on g8 or g7. b5 is a queenside move while your king is in danger. Kh8 lets you play Rg8 and fight for the g-file. Always check your opponent's checks before starting your own plan.
concept: missed mating attack on the g-file

coach_says: Black's queen on h3 and pawn on h2 have your king trapped, and the knight on d4 is the piece that finishes it: Nf3 covers g1, then the queen comes to g1 and the pawn promotes with mate. Bxd4 removes that knight and you were winning. cxd6 grabs a pawn but lets Nf3 in. When your king is under attack, first get rid of the attacker that makes the threat work.
concept: remove the key attacking knight

coach_says: You are a lot of material down, so every move needs to make Black work. Be3 pulls the bishop back without a threat, and Black uses the time for e5 and Ne7 to finish developing with the king safe. Rfe1, hitting the queen, or Qc7, attacking b7 and the bishop on d7, keep Black busy. When behind, prefer moves that attack something.
concept: passive retreat when behind
also: gain time by attacking the queen

coach_says: You had two ways to take on c4. Bxc4 dxc4 Nxc4 wins a pawn and puts your knight on c4, heading for d6, a hole Black can't cover now their dark-squared bishop is gone. Nxc4 dxc4 swaps your developed knight and leaves a Black pawn on c4 that blocks your bishop. When you can recapture with two pieces, think about which piece you want left on the board.
concept: choosing the right recapture

coach_says: Your g7 bishop is aiming down the long diagonal at the knights on d4 and c3. The c3 knight is unprotected, so if the d4 knight moves, Bxc3+ is check. White hasn't castled or developed the c1 bishop yet. That was the moment to add pressure with Nfd5, hitting c3, before White plays Bb2 and castles. Castling is a fine move, but it gives White the one tempo they needed.
concept: exploit the long-diagonal pin quickly

coach_says: When you recapture with a pawn, check which files it opens. hxg3 opens the h-file for your rook on h1, and together with the bishop on d3 that hits h7: Rxh7 wins a pawn. fxg3 opens the f-file instead, where nothing is happening for you. Capturing toward the centre is a good rule, but a concrete target beats a general rule.
concept: recapture to open a file for the rook
also: rook and bishop battery on h7

coach_says: You are a piece down, and White's queen on g5 is deep in your half. Kick it with your pawns: h6, and after Qh4 then g5, with g4 next to hit the knight on f3. Every kick gains time and can win material back. Bb4 attacks a knight that is well defended, and White answers with Bd3 and Qf5 to trade queens, which suits the side with more material.
concept: kick the queen with pawns

coach_says: Black's bishop on c5 is pointing at e3 and g1, which stops you castling short and pressures your centre. d4 takes the centre and hits the bishop,, so it has to move again or be swapped, and it shuts the bishop off from e3 and g1. Bc3 is slow and lets Black keep the bishop where it is. In the opening, look for pawn moves that take the centre and attack a piece at the same time.
concept: take the centre with tempo (d4)

coach_says: Your bishop on d7 was shielding the queen on d8 from the rook on d1. After Bxc6 the d-file is open, so the d6 pawn is pinned to your queen and no longer really defends e5: Nxe5 is possible because dxe5 Rxd8. Recapturing with bxc6 keeps the bishop on d7, controls d5 and opens the b-file toward White's king on c1. When choosing a recapture, check what the moving piece was blocking.
concept: recapture opened a pin on the d-file

coach_says: In this Traxler line the point of Bc5 is Bxf2+ first. Taking with check drags the king out: after Kxf2 Nxe4+ your pieces attack it, and after Kf1 the king can never castle and you get Qe7 with good play anyway. Playing Qe7 straight away lets White keep the king safe and just take the rook on h8. When you have a forcing check that opens the enemy king, play it before the quiet move.
concept: check first: Bxf2+ to drag the king
